clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive urea cycle disorder caused by deficiency of argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS1), which condenses citrulline and aspartate; the block causes hyperammonaemia and marked accumulation of citrulline.
Classic neonatal form presents within the first days of life with poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, hypotonia progressing to encephalopathy, seizures and coma from severe hyperammonaemia.

Later-onset and milder forms occur, presenting in childhood or adulthood with episodic hyperammonaemia, recurrent vomiting, behavioural change or migraine-like episodes triggered by catabolic stress or high protein intake.
Plasma amino acids show grossly elevated citrulline with low or absent argininosuccinate, distinguishing it from argininosuccinic aciduria; orotic acid is typically raised in urine.

Acute hyperammonaemia is a medical emergency: stop protein intake, reverse catabolism with high-energy glucose (with intralipid), and use nitrogen-scavenging agents and arginine, escalating to dialysis for severe or refractory elevation.
Long-term management combines a protein-restricted diet with arginine supplementation and nitrogen scavengers; liver transplantation corrects the enzymatic defect in severely affected patients.
Peak ammonia during a crisis correlates with neurological outcome, so speed of ammonia lowering is critical to prevent permanent brain injury.
Distinguish from citrin deficiency (citrullinaemia type 2), which has a different biochemical and clinical profile and different dietary implications.
reference.pathophysiology: Argininosuccinate synthetase catalyses the third step of the urea cycle, joining citrulline with aspartate to form argininosuccinate, the reaction that incorporates the second waste nitrogen atom. When ASS1 activity is deficient, flux through the urea cycle is blocked at this point, so ammonia is not converted to urea and accumulates in the blood, while citrulline builds up proximal to the block and aspartate-derived nitrogen cannot be disposed of. The excess carbamoyl phosphate that accumulates upstream is diverted into pyrimidine synthesis, generating orotic acid. Hyperammonaemia is directly neurotoxic: ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier, drives glutamine accumulation in astrocytes with osmotic swelling and cerebral oedema, and disturbs neurotransmission and cerebral energy metabolism, producing encephalopathy that can progress to irreversible damage or death. Because arginine cannot be synthesised endogenously when the cycle is interrupted, it becomes a conditionally essential amino acid, and its deficiency further limits any residual cycle function. Severity tracks with residual enzyme activity, ranging from the fulminant neonatal presentation to attenuated late-onset disease that manifests only during metabolic stress.
additionalDifferentials: Other urea cycle disorders (ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency, argininosuccinic aciduria)
Neonatal sepsis and other causes of neonatal encephalopathy
additionalInvestigations: Plasma ammonia (urgent, correctly sampled and transported on ice)
Plasma amino acid profile showing markedly elevated citrulline with low argininosuccinate and arginine
Urine orotic acid and organic acids
Blood gas, glucose and lactate to assess metabolic status
Molecular genetic testing of the ASS1 gene
Newborn screening acylcarnitine and amino acid results where available
Neuroimaging in prolonged or severe encephalopathy to assess cerebral oedema
redFlags: Rapidly rising or markedly elevated plasma ammonia with encephalopathy
Deteriorating consciousness, seizures or signs of raised intracranial pressure
Neonate with unexplained lethargy, poor feeding and respiratory alkalosis
Recurrent unexplained vomiting with altered behaviour in an older child or adult
Failure of ammonia to fall despite scavengers, indicating need for dialysis
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends chiefly on the severity and duration of neonatal hyperammonaemia; early aggressive treatment improves survival but neurodevelopmental sequelae are common after severe crises. Later-onset forms have a better prognosis when triggers are avoided and crises are treated promptly, and liver transplantation can be curative of the metabolic defect.
pitfalls: Delaying ammonia measurement or mishandling the sample, leading to false results and missed emergencies
Attributing neonatal collapse to sepsis alone and overlooking a urea cycle disorder
Confusing type 1 with citrin deficiency, which carries different dietary and prognostic implications
Under-treating catabolism, so continued protein breakdown sustains hyperammonaemia
Failing to provide arginine, which is conditionally essential in this disorder
references: Standard textbook of inborn errors of metabolism
International urea cycle disorder management guidelines
management: Acute hyperammonaemia treated as an emergency by stopping protein intake, reversing catabolism with high-energy glucose and intravenous lipid, and giving nitrogen-scavenging agents such as sodium benzoate and sodium phenylbutyrate with intravenous arginine
Haemodialysis or haemofiltration for severe or refractory hyperammonaemia
Long-term protein-restricted diet with arginine supplementation and oral nitrogen scavengers
Avoidance of catabolic triggers and use of an emergency sick-day regimen during intercurrent illness
Monitoring of plasma ammonia, amino acids, growth and neurodevelopment
Liver transplantation for severely affected patients or those with recurrent crises
Coordinated care through a specialist metabolic team and metabolic dietitian
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive ASS1 disorder with family and newborn screening
